problem:
Aldergate Bank runs a legacy supplier payment process that has grown by accretion over a decade. A corporate customer sends a payment file, operations staff print exception lists, re-key corrected details into three different screens, phone the customer for missing information, and then release the file late in the day. The process works, in the sense that most payments eventually leave, but it is slow, error-prone and expensive: re-keying introduces mistakes, nobody can say how long a file spends at each step, and the team cannot tell whether a delay comes from bad data, a system limit or a staffing gap. The head of operations has asked for the process to be optimised, but has not said which outcome matters most: faster release, fewer errors, lower cost, or better customer visibility.

The business analyst assigned to the work inherits a process nobody has mapped end to end. Each team describes only its own step, the documented procedure is three versions out of date, and two workarounds exist that nobody has written down. Meanwhile a recent client escalation complained that a changed process step disrupted the client's own operations, which shows that improvement work can make things worse if it is done without evidence. The learner must map the as-is process, quantify the pain with real measures, design a to-be process with controls that survive contact with real files, and validate the change with the people who run it and the customers who depend on it.
solution:
Begin by observing the work as performed, not as documented: follow real files from intake to release, time each step, and record every workaround, handoff and re-key. Quantify the pain with measures the business can compare: straight-through processing rate, repair rate by defect type, average and worst-case cycle time per step, rework hours, error rate after release, and customer contacts per file. Segment defects by root cause and source so the redesign fixes causes rather than symptoms, and identify which defects should be prevented at source through upstream validation instead of repaired downstream.

Design the to-be process around the measured bottlenecks: single capture with validation at source, no re-keying, itemised file outcomes, and a repair workbench with maker-checker control for sensitive changes. Keep the controls that the evidence shows actually catch errors, and remove only steps the data proves add no value. Validate the design with operators through a walkthrough of real files, and with customers through the changed touchpoints, including status visibility and repair requests. Pilot on a small volume, compare the same measures before and after, and only then roll out with training, updated procedures and a rollback plan.

decision.question: Aldergate Bank's legacy supplier payment process is slow and error-prone, with re-keying across three screens and undocumented workarounds. The head of operations wants it optimised but has not prioritised speed, accuracy, cost or visibility. You are the business analyst asked to redesign it.

options.label: A
options.detail: Redesign the process from the documented procedure, since it is the official record of how the work should be done.

options.label: B
options.detail: Remove the manual exception checks first to speed up release, and add controls later if errors rise.

options.label: C
options.detail: Map the as-is process as actually performed, quantify pain at each step, design the to-be process with controls, and validate it with operators and customers.

options.label: D
options.detail: Automate the current steps exactly as they are, because automation alone will remove the delays.

decisionRationale: Option C is correct because improvement must start from the real process and measured pain, not from an outdated document. Option A designs around a procedure three versions out of date. Option D automates waste and undocumented workarounds. Option B removes controls before knowing which errors they catch, which trades speed for uncontrolled risk.

steps.title: Observe live file processing and interview operators at each handoff
Provide cycle time, repair and error measures for the last three months
Map as-is process with timings, workarounds and pain points
Segment defects by root cause and prioritise fixes by impact
Design to-be process with single capture, validation and repair workbench
Walk through to-be design with operators using real files
Pilot to-be process, compare measures and report go or no-go

happy: The to-be process runs on a pilot volume with a higher straight-through processing rate, lower repair rate and shorter cycle time than the as-is baseline, measured on the same metrics. Operators confirm the new steps are workable, customers receive itemised outcomes and clear repair guidance, and the rollout proceeds with updated procedures and training.

negative.title: Client escalates that the change disrupted operations
negative.detail: A changed step makes a customer process harder or impossible. Acknowledge impact without defensiveness, establish facts and a workaround, name an owner and an update time, then investigate root cause separately from service recovery.

negative.title: Automation reproduces the old errors faster
negative.detail: The to-be design automated a step that was itself the defect source. Stop the pilot, trace defects to the step that creates them, and fix the source before resuming.

negative.title: Operators keep using the old workaround
negative.detail: The new step does not fit a real case the design missed. Observe the workaround, understand the case it serves, and change the design or the procedure rather than blaming operators.

negative.title: Improvement in one metric harms another
negative.detail: Faster release raises the post-release error rate. Report both measures together, restore the control that caught the errors, and re-balance speed against accuracy with the process owner.

technical: Record the as-is and to-be maps with version, date and owner, and keep the measurement definitions stable so before and after figures are comparable. Store defect segmentation with file ID, transaction ID, defect type, source and resolution so trends can be re-run. Log every repair with operator, field changed, old and new value, timestamp and checker, and keep the original file and the corrected file linked by the same file reference for audit.

fields.name: Count of accepted and rejected items

fields.name: Remittance information carried from the file item

accounting: Each accepted file item produces one debit to the customer account and one credit transfer; rejected items produce no financial movement. Repaired items must not lose their original traceability, and a repaired item that is resubmitted must not create a duplicate debit. Operations need a repair worklist with ageing and service levels, a control total that reconciles file value to debits posted, and a daily break report for items accepted but not settled. Staffing for the repair queue must be sized from the measured defect rate, not from optimism about the new validation.

scenarios.given: a legacy process with undocumented workarounds,
scenarios.then: it reflects the process as actually performed with timings and handoffs.

scenarios.given: defect data segmented by root cause,
scenarios.then: fixes target the highest-impact causes and state which defects are prevented at source.

scenarios.given: a pilot of the to-be process,
scenarios.when: the same measures are compared before and after,
scenarios.then: the improvement decision rests on measured evidence.

questions.question: Why must improvement start from the as-is process as actually performed?
options: The documented procedure is out of date and workarounds are undocumented
The documented procedure is always accurate
questions.explanation: The documented procedure is three versions out of date and two workarounds exist that nobody has written down, so only observation reveals the real process.

questions.question: Which measure best shows whether repair work is falling?
options: Straight-through processing rate and repair rate by defect type
questions.explanation: Straight-through processing rate and repair rate by defect type show directly how much work flows cleanly and where defects concentrate.

questions.question: What should happen first when a client escalates that a change disrupted operations?
options: Ask the client to wait for the next release
Confirm impact, containment, owner and next update time
questions.explanation: Service recovery comes first: impact, a safe workaround, a named owner and an update time, with root cause and accountability handled afterwards.

questions.question: Why is maker-checker control kept for sensitive repairs?
options: It is required for all fields
It prevents a single operator error from changing payment meaning
questions.explanation: Maker-checker control on sensitive changes prevents one person's error or misuse from altering the amount, beneficiary or account of a payment.
